title: Carrying Out a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 3.15 Carrying Out a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence
intro: After this lesson you can calculate expected counts, the chi-square statistic and its degrees of freedom, find a p-value from a chi-square distribution, interpret it, and write a conclusion in context.

moments.title: Seven steps
moments.text: Name, parameter, hypotheses, conditions, test statistic, p-value, conclusion. This topic carries out the last three.

moments.title: Hypotheses by test type
moments.text: Independence: no association in the population. Homogeneity: the same distribution across the populations.

moments.title: Check the 10% condition for each sample
moments.text: Do it once per sample. Skip it for a randomized experiment.

moments.title: Expected counts at least 5
moments.text: Check expected counts, not observed counts.

moments.title: Expected count
moments.text: $\dfrac{(\text{row total})(\text{column total})}{\text{table total}}$ for each cell inside the table.

moments.title: Chi-square statistic
moments.text: $\chi^2=\sum\dfrac{(O-E)^2}{E}$ over every cell, excluding the totals.

moments.title: Large $\chi^2$ means observed counts far from expected
moments.text: A larger statistic gives a smaller p-value.

moments.title: p-value for chi-square
moments.text: The probability of a statistic this large or larger, assuming $H_0$ is true. The test is always in the right tail.

moments.title: Moderate statistic, large p-value
moments.text: $\chi^2=1.258$ with 5 degrees of freedom gives a very large p-value.

moments.title: Large statistic, small p-value
moments.text: $\chi^2=13.567$ with 2 degrees of freedom gives p about 0.0011.

moments.title: Conclusion in context
moments.text: Compare the p-value to $\alpha$, decide, and answer the investigative question about the population or populations.

moments.title: Gym members: age and workout type
moments.text: One random sample, two variables: independence. $\chi^2=15.223$, 4 degrees of freedom, p about 0.0043.

moments.title: What the expected counts mean
moments.text: They show what the table would look like if there were no association.

moments.title: Why a small p-value is evidence of association
moments.text: The observed table would be very unlikely if there were no association.

moments.title: Pet ownership in three cities
moments.text: Three samples (90, 80 and 80), one variable: homogeneity.

moments.title: Expected count by hand
moments.text: A multiple-choice question may ask how many in a group would own a cat if the distribution were the same.

sections.title: What does the p-value tell you?

cards.name: Reject $H_0$
cards.text: p-value $\le\alpha$. Convincing evidence of an association (independence) or a difference in distributions (homogeneity).

cards.name: Fail to reject
cards.text: p-value $>\alpha$. Not convincing evidence. Never say the null is true.

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: The video reads the p-value for $\chi^2=13.567$ with 2 degrees of freedom as 0.0001. The correct value is about 0.0011. Either way the decision is the same.

sections.title: Compute the statistic and p-value
sections.intro: Work cell by cell, add the contributions, then use the right tail of the chi-square distribution with the correct degrees of freedom.
steps: Expected count for each cell: row total times column total over the grand total.
Contribution for each cell: $(O-E)^2/E$. Do not include the totals.
Add the contributions to get $\chi^2$, and find $df=(r-1)(c-1)$.
The p-value is the area to the right of $\chi^2$. Compare to $\alpha$ and conclude in context.

traps.title: Conclusion for independence
traps.weak: We reject the null because the p-value is small.
traps.better: Because the p-value of 0.0023 is less than $\alpha=0.05$, we reject $H_0$. There is convincing evidence of an association between age group and preferred workout type for all members of the gym.

traps.title: Conclusion for homogeneity
traps.better: Because the p-value of 0.087 is greater than 0.05, we fail to reject $H_0$. There is not convincing evidence that the distribution of commute type differs between the two cities for all commuters.

traps.title: Including the totals
traps.weak: Add a contribution for every row and column total.
traps.better: Use only the cells inside the table. The totals are not observed counts for a category pair.

traps.title: Using both tails
traps.weak: Double the area for a two-sided test.
traps.better: A chi-square test is always in the right tail. Large values of $\chi^2$ give evidence for the alternative.

questions.stem: A two-way table has 4 rows and 3 columns of categories. How many degrees of freedom does the chi-square test have?
why: This is the number of cells.

questions.stem: A chi-square test has $\chi^2=4.883$ with 2 degrees of freedom, and the p-value is 0.087. At $\alpha=0.05$, which conclusion is correct?
opts: Reject $H_0$; there is evidence of an association.
Fail to reject $H_0$; there is not convincing evidence of an association.
why: Reject only when the p-value is at most $\alpha$.
Correct. The p-value is greater than $\alpha$, so fail to reject $H_0$.
A test never proves the null hypothesis.

questions.stem: In a chi-square test of homogeneity, 90 residents of City A were asked their pet type (cat, dog or other). The total number of cat owners across the three cities is 100 out of 250 pet owners. If the distribution were the same in all cities, about how many of the 90 City A pet owners would own a cat?
why: This is 100 out of 250 applied to 100 people.
This uses a rate of 1/3 for each pet type.
This is not related to the table totals.

questions.stem: Which statement is the correct interpretation of the p-value in a chi-square test?
opts: The probability that the alternative hypothesis is true
The proportion of cells with large expected counts
The probability that the null hypothesis is true
The probability of getting a chi-square statistic this large or larger, assuming the null hypothesis is true
why: The p-value does not give the probability of the alternative.
The p-value is not about expected counts.
The p-value is calculated assuming $H_0$ is true; it is not the probability of $H_0$.
Correct. This is the definition, in the direction of the alternative (the right tail).

sections.title: Free-response practice
sections.prompt: A transport survey took independent random samples of 100 commuters in City A and 100 commuters in City B. Each commuter reported bike, bus or car. City A: 45 bike, 30 bus, 25 car. City B: 30 bike, 40 bus, 30 car. Is there convincing evidence at $\alpha=0.05$ that the distribution of commute type is different in the two cities?
parts: (a) State the test and the hypotheses.
(b) Verify the conditions, including the expected counts.
(c) Calculate the test statistic, degrees of freedom and p-value.
sample: (a) A chi-square test for homogeneity. $H_0$: the distribution of commute type is the same for commuters in City A and City B. $H_a$: the distribution of commute type is different.
(b) Independent random samples of 100 commuters each (under 10% of each city). Expected counts: bike 37.5 and 37.5, bus 35 and 35, car 27.5 and 27.5. All are at least 5.
(d) The p-value 0.087 is greater than 0.05, so we fail to reject $H_0$. There is not convincing evidence that the distribution of commute type differs between City A and City B.
checklist: (b) All six expected counts at least 5
(d) Conclusion in context without claiming no difference
